prompt: I'm learning linear algebra and want a visual that builds intuition for eigenvectors and eigenvalues. Show a 2D linear map transforming the unit circle into an ellipse and highlight the eigen-directions with scaled vectors. Then extend to 3D to illustrate how the matrix decomposes into eigen-directions, with a live parameter sweep showing convergence or divergence. Include multiple scenes with transitions, 3D Axes, TracedPath for trajectories, and MathTex labels for the formulas. Relate the visuals to real-world stability directions and compare with a non-diagonalizable case to emphasize intuition.

In a graduate linear algebra visualization, demonstrate eigen decomposition of a symmetric 3×3 matrix. Show how A acts on the unit sphere to yield an ellipsoid with principal axes along the eigenvectors and edge lengths given by the eigenvalues. Animate A = Q Λ Q^T to build intuition, with the camera orbiting to reveal orientation and a moving vector trace to illustrate the transformation. Include a perturbation sweep to show eigenvalue sensitivity and a short comparison to PCA on a small synthetic dataset.

I'm learning an undergrad signal processing course and want a visual tour of the FFT.
Begin with a time-domain waveform, then animate the butterfly network to show how the spectrum is built.
Display magnitude and phase plots evolving in tandem, and compare with the direct DFT for small N.
Include a short audio example to illustrate windowing effects, with camera moves that zoom into the spectrum.
Keep the pacing intuitive but rigorous, with intuition first, then the math, and clear captions.

I'm learning an undergrad course on numerical linear algebra and want a visual explanation of SVD.
Show geometrically how a matrix A transforms the unit circle into an ellipse, with singular vectors as axes and Σ as scaling.
Then decompose A as UΣV^T and illustrate the transformation step by step, including a noisy perturbation to show conditioning.
Include multiple scenes: constructing the ellipse, applying A to the circle, and a real-world data example to motivate use.
I’d like the animation to have clear pacing, smooth transitions, and both intuition and rigorous definitions.

I'm learning undergrad ML students and want a vivid visualization of optimization dynamics.
Create an animation comparing gradient descent with and without momentum on a 2D non-convex loss, with both contour plots and a 3D surface view.
Show how different learning rates affect convergence, oscillations, and overshoot, and include a quick intuition before the math followed by a brief derivation.
Use multiple scenes, smooth transitions, annotations, and a small numerical example illustrating convergence time.

I'm learning linear algebra and want a visual that builds intuition for eigenvectors and eigenvalues. Show a general 2x2 linear transformation acting on the plane, with vectors colored by their stretching, then highlight the eigenlines and their scale factors. Then present a 3D symmetric matrix, decompose it into eigenvectors and eigenvalues, and illustrate spectral decomposition with an animated rotation and scale. Demonstrate a practical application by projecting sample data onto principal components and showing variance explained. Include multiple scenes, camera moves, transitions, and a clear derivation of the characteristic equation motivated by area/volume scaling, before the algebra.

I'm an instructor designing a Manim video for a sophomore linear algebra class; prerequisite: vectors, matrix multiplication, and basic eigen/SVD ideas. Create a visual that builds intuition for singular value decomposition: A = U Σ V^T with singular values as scaling along principal axes. Show multiple scenes: a 2D/3D linear map acting on shapes (unit circle to ellipse), then reconstruction with rank-k approximations, and a tiny data cloud compressed into lower dimensions. I want intuition first, then equations on screen, with smooth scene transitions and camera moves; include a plot of the singular value spectrum and discuss truncation error and PCA intuition. End with a brief note on real-world applications and when SVD is especially useful.

I teach an upper-level linear algebra course and want a rich Manim animation to build intuition for QR decomposition and least squares.
Show Gram–Schmidt on a 3D point cloud, visualize orthogonality step by step, then fit a plane to data with least-squares and animate the residuals.
Include multiple scenes: decomposition, iterative improvement, and a comparison with the true solution; use 3D axes, animated equations, and a moving camera.
Audience: advanced undergraduates; prerequisites: linear algebra and calculus; depth: rigorous yet intuitive; pacing and transitions to clarify the derivation; real-world applications in data fitting and computer vision.

I'm learning optimization and want a visual comparison of gradient descent, momentum, and Adam on a nonconvex loss.
Show a 3D loss landscape with three trajectories starting from the same point, plus a 2D zoom near the minima.
Include a parameter sweep over learning rate and momentum/beta, with animated plots showing convergence time and oscillations.
Add intuitive explanations and a short visual derivation of the update rules, using realistic numbers so the scene feels authentic.

I'm learning optimization and want a visual that clarifies why gradient descent struggles near saddle points. Display a non-convex 3D loss surface with several trajectories under different learning rates, and compare with momentum. I'd like intuition first, then the exact update equations shown in sync as the path evolves, highlighting regions where step size helps or hurts. Include multiple scenes with zooms, a side plot of loss over time, and a brief demonstration of how preconditioning changes the path.

I'm learning linear algebra to undergraduates and want a visual that unpacks singular value decomposition.
Show how a 2D/3D linear map stretches and rotates vectors into principal axes, with animated ellipsoids and a moving camera.
Include step-by-step intuition, then derive A = U Σ V^T visually, plus a numeric example with a 3x3 matrix and a dynamic plot of singular values as you tweak A.
I want multiple scenes: initial grid under transformation, decomposition stage, and a comparison with eigen decomposition for symmetric cases.
Pacing should be moderate; use 3D axes, TracedPath of a chosen vector, and a small interactive prompt asking viewers to guess the effect of changing a singular value.

I'm learning a linear algebra module to upper-undergraduates and want a visual that makes eigen decomposition intuition-rich. Show a 2D rotation-scaling example to reveal invariant eigenvectors, then a 3D view of a symmetric matrix acting on a shape so eigen-directions stand out. Animate how any vector decomposes into the eigenbasis with projection lengths scaled by the eigenvalues, including a shot of repeated application. Include a concise comparison with SVD for non-symmetric matrices and a PCA-style real-world dataset example. Use multiple scenes, smooth transitions, captions, and intuitive cues; let there be pacing that favors understanding and visual intuition.

Curious about how gradient descent navigates a non-convex loss. Show a 2D contour of a toy loss with multiple minima, then animate several optimization runs from different starting points using varied learning rates. I want to trace the paths, highlight saddle points, and visualize step updates as arrows or paths, with a switch to a 3D surface view for intuition. Include camera movement, pacing, and a concise narration that explains why larger steps can overshoot.

For first-year calculus students, I want an intuitive animation that shows the derivative as a limit of secant slopes. Begin with a smooth function, animate secants approaching the tangent, then reveal the derivative formula and plot f'(x) alongside. Include examples like x^2 and sin x, and a real-world interpretation such as instantaneous velocity. Keep visuals clean on a 2D graph with a moving point, trailing path, labeled axes, and transitions from intuition to rigor, paced for pause-and-reflect moments.

Explain eigenvectors and eigenvalues in geometric terms for undergraduates.
Show a 2D linear transformation: start with the unit circle, map to an ellipse under a 2×2 matrix, then highlight the invariant lines along eigenvectors and how the ellipse stretches by the eigenvalues.
Include a quick, visual derivation Av=λv, with area intuition.
I want multiple scenes, a slider to rotate/scale the matrix, color coding, and transitions between the geometric view and a short real-world example like stability in a mass-spring system.

I’m learning a differential geometry unit and want a visual that explains Green's theorem in the plane.
Show a smooth vector field on a region, and animate how the line integral around a simple closed curve equals the double integral of the curl over the interior.
Include multiple scenes: boundary tracing with real-time accumulation, shading of the interior, and a side plot comparing both sides as the curve deforms.
I’d like intuitive narration first, then the formal derivation, then a quick real-world application like fluid circulation around an obstacle.
Use camera moves to focus on the boundary and then the interior and highlight the geometric meaning behind the equality.

I'm learning advanced optimization to upper-level undergrads. Create a multi-scene animation visualizing gradient descent on a non-convex loss with at least two minima. Show a 3D surface and a 2D contour, with gradient-descent paths for different learning rates, including momentum, so we can compare convergence and saddle-point escape. Include a side plot of gradient norm over iterations and a zoomed-in view of curvature near the minima, using numerical simulation to generate the trajectories. Provide intuitive explanations before the equations and enable smooth scene transitions that highlight the intuition behind each concept.

I'm learning upper-level CS and want a vivid visualization of Kruskal's algorithm.
Show a weighted undirected graph and animate the edge selections that build the minimum spanning tree, highlighting each decision as it's made.
Include a running union-find visualization, a cost timeline, and a quick sweep over different graph sizes to compare performance and MST weight.
Begin with an intuition for why greediness works, then derive the algorithm and finish with a concise proof sketch and a real-world analogy.
Structure the video as multiple scenes with smooth transitions, color-coded statuses, and camera moves that emphasize the changes in the MST.

I need a visual explanation of the spectral theorem for linear algebra, aimed at advanced undergrads.
Show a symmetric matrix acting on 3D vectors, with eigenvectors as fixed directions and arrows colored by component contributions.
Animate the decomposition of any vector into its eigenbasis and the corresponding projections, then illustrate how the transformation acts as a scale along those axes.
Include multiple scenes: original vector field, basis change, and a side-by-side comparison of original and transformed shapes.
I want intuitive motion first, then derive the formula on screen with a visual derivation of the diagonalization process.

I'm learning undergrads who know calculus and basic linear algebra, but I still struggle to visualize gradient descent on rugged surfaces.
Visualize a bumpy 2D loss landscape with multiple minima and saddles, and animate the gradient-descent path from several starting points.
Include both the continuous gradient flow and the discrete update steps, plus a parameter sweep over learning rate and momentum.
I want four scenes: a 3D terrain view, a transparent overlaid path, a zoomed-in close-up of a chosen minima, and a side-by-side comparison with and without momentum, with intuition first and equations afterward.

I'm learning signals and want a visual that ties time-domain signals to their frequency content. Show a simple sine, then add harmonics and demonstrate how the FFT magnitude changes. Include a short-time Fourier transform spectrogram and a discussion of window length, leakage, and resolution. Provide multiple scenes: waveforms, spectra, and a 3D surface of magnitude vs frequency and time. Wrap with intuition diagrams before the equations and a quick real-world example like audio or ECG.

In a signals course, I want a rich visualization of Fourier series convergence for a square wave.

Show partial sums building up and the Gibbs phenomenon near the jump, with the spectrum represented as bars that shrink into the time signal as more terms are added.

Create multiple scenes: (a) time-domain reconstruction with a dynamic error plot, (b) the evolving frequency spectrum, (c) a close-up zoom at a discontinuity; include a smooth camera orbit and pan.

Explain why convergence is in L2 but not uniform, and relate to practical audio synthesis and reconstruction from samples, with intuitive narration and precise formulas appearing on screen.

Target audience: undergraduate math/engineering; depth: intermediate; pacing: moderate; visual style: clean with blue/teal palette and crisp math typography.

Curious about eigenvalues and eigenvectors? I want a geometric visualization for a 2x2 matrix: animate the plane under the linear map, highlight eigen-directions and their scaling, and compare with non-eigen directions. Then visualize the quadratic form x^T A x as a 3D surface and contours to show how eigenvalues shape the ridges. I'd like a quick intuition before the equations, and a brief discussion of diagonalizable vs non-diagonalizable cases with a real-world analogy.

As an undergraduate learning linear algebra, I want a visualization of the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices.
Show how any vector decomposes into eigenvectors and how the matrix scales along those directions, with the eigenspaces highlighted in 3D.
I’d like a sequence of scenes: intuition first, then the algebra, then a concrete 4x4 example with explicit eigen-decomposition and animated transformation.
Include a brief contrast with a non-symmetric matrix to illustrate why the theorem fails there, and relate the result to PCA and least squares.
Use smooth camera motion, multiple plots, rotating axes, and animated formulas that derive the key steps.

I'm learning undergraduate linear algebra and want a visual explanation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
Animate a 2×2 real matrix acting on the plane: the unit circle deforms into an ellipse, with the eigen-directions highlighted and stretched by their eigenvalues.
Then illustrate a rotation–scaling intuition and compare to the general case, using multiple scenes and a side plot showing the norm ratio along eigen-directions.
Include color-coded vectors, axes, a camera orbit, and guidance from intuition before the equations; prerequisites are basic matrix algebra.

I'm learning optimization to upper-undergraduate students with calculus and linear algebra background.
Create a visual of gradient descent on a non-convex loss with multiple minima; show the 3D surface and the path from different starting points.
Highlight how step size and momentum affect convergence; include animated updates and annotations of the update rule.
Provide intuition before the equations, then compare convergence for several learning rates; end with a real-world intuition.

For an introductory to intermediate audience (calculus/linear algebra), animate gradient descent on a non-convex loss and explain why it can overshoot or stall.
Show a 3D surface, a 2D contour map, and the path of the parameter vector with varying learning rates and momentum.
Include a sweep of learning rates, a comparison with Newton's method, and a demonstration of convergence criteria via a moving horizon.
Before equations, develop geometric intuition (steepest descent along normals); then visualize the update rule and the Hessian's role; add a real-world example.
End with practical tips and potential misconceptions, using multiple scenes, camera transitions, and animated formulas.

Curious about how SVD reshapes data in PCA-like fashion. Can you animate a 3D point cloud undergoing a sequence: first the original cloud, then its alignment along the left singular vectors, then scaling by the singular values, and finally projecting back to 3D with a low-rank approximation. I want to see the reconstruction error decrease as we include more components, with the camera orbiting the data and smooth transitions between stages. Include intuitive explanations before the math, then derive the core formula visually.

I'm learning undergrad numerical analysis. Create a visual demonstration of Newton's method for root finding on a non-linear function. Show the 2D plot of f(x), its tangent at the current iterate, and the sequence of iterates from several starting points; highlight basins of attraction. Include a short error-progress plot and a side-by-side animation of the update rule x_{n+1}=x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n). Use multiple scenes with zooms into the curve near roots, and switch to a 3D view that overlays the surface z=f(x) with the tangent plane along the path. Compare a well-behaved polynomial and a problematic function to illustrate convergence vs divergence.

I'm learning undergrads and want a visually rich animation of the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices.
Animate how a sphere is stretched into an ellipsoid by M, then reveal invariant eigen-directions with M = PDP^T and the diagonal scaling D in those coordinates.
Include a parameter sweep showing how eigenvalues/eigenvectors evolve as M is perturbed, plus intuition before the equations and a geometric derivation afterward.
Context: principal axes in stress analysis or PCA; pacing, smooth transitions, and 3D visuals with Axes/ThreeDAxes, Braces, MathTex, and TracedPath.
The video should help students connect linear algebra intuition to rigorous results.

In a graduate course on numerical linear algebra, I'd like a visually rich explanation of SVD on a noisy 2D data cloud. Animate the data points, show the principal directions (singular vectors) and how truncating to k singular values reconstructs the data, with intuitive before/after visuals. Include multiple scenes: a scatter plot, a 3D bar chart of singular values, and a live reconstruction as k increases, plus a rotating view to compare orientations. Also sweep noise levels and show the reconstruction error as a function of k, culminating in a geometric intuition for the Eckart–Young theorem.

I'm learning a graduate-level optimization module and want a visual that explains why SGD behaves differently from full-batch gradient descent in non-convex landscapes. Show a high-dimensional loss surface projected to 3D with a 2D contour, and animate trajectories for SGD, Momentum, and Adam across multiple basins. Include scenes that zoom into saddles, then sweep hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size) to illustrate convergence behavior and escape routes. Provide intuition before equations, then visually derive the update steps and show the effect on the loss over iterations. Target audience: graduate students; prerequisites: calculus, linear algebra, probability; pacing and visuals should be rich and engaging, with clear scene transitions and multiple representations of the same idea.

I’m learning sophomore linear algebra and want a concise Manim animation that builds intuition for SVD. Visualize A acting on the unit sphere to produce an ellipsoid, then decompose into U Σ V^T and animate how the principal axes and singular values arise. Include a quick contrast with eigen decomposition for a symmetric A, and a parameter sweep showing how Σ changes as A varies toward different conditioning. Use multiple scenes with clean 3D plots, camera motion to hover over the axes, and transitions that explain the intuition before the equations. Real-world tie-in: show how SVD underpins image compression and data reduction, with a brief example.

I'm learning undergraduates linear algebra and want a Manim animation visualizing Gaussian elimination on a 3x3 system.
Show the matrix with pivot elements highlighted, then perform the row operations step by step, and finish with back-substitution to reveal the solution vector.
Include separate scenes: initial setup, the elimination path, and a brief comparison to LU decomposition.
Emphasize intuition, common pitfalls, and numerical stability, using clear color coding and smooth, didactic pacing.

I'm an upper-level linear algebra teacher; I want a Manim animation that builds intuition for spectral decomposition of a 3×3 matrix.
Show the matrix acting on a field of vectors, with eigenvectors unchanged in direction and scaled by eigenvalues, and then visualize A = PDP^{-1} in a concrete example.
Include multiple scenes: initial unsystematic vectors, projection onto the eigenbasis, then the transformed vectors, with color-coded directions.
I’d like sliders for eigenvalues, a rotating camera, and a side plot showing condition number or spread of eigenvalues to discuss stability and intuition.
